task.instruction: Read the latest health-related news article published on BBC News and summarize the key points discussed.

final_answer:
**Article:** "Scientists think our recent ancestors may have run hotter – but why?" by Sandy Ong, BBC Future (published ~1 day ago, 30 Oct 2026) — the lead story on BBC Health.

**The core finding:** Average human body temperature has declined measurably over the past 150 years. In the 1860s the German physician Carl Wunderlich collected over a million armpit readings from 25,000 patients over 15 years and set the benchmark of 37C (98.6F) for healthy adults, with 38C (100.4F) signalling fever. That figure became a near-universal diagnostic standard. But modern data tells a different story: Stanford's Julie Parsonnet analysed three large datasets covering nearly 190,000 people measured between 1862 and 2017 and found today's normal is closer to 36.4C (97.5F). American men now run about 0.59C cooler than in the early 19th Century. The trend isn't confined to rich countries — the Tsimane, a semi-nomadic Amazonian community, averaged around 37C in the early 2000s but had fallen to 36.5C by 2018 after two decades of rapid socioeconomic change.

**Why the drop? Two competing explanations.** Parsonnet argues it reflects healthier populations: in Wunderlich's day life expectancy was 38 years and chronic infections — tuberculosis, dysentery, rheumatic fever, osteomyelitis, poor dental care — kept immune systems constantly burning calories, and "calories are another word for heat." Better sanitation, vaccines, shoes (fewer hookworm infections) and controlled indoor climates mean we now live in a "thermal-neutral zone" where the body doesn't have to work to hold its temperature. Medical historian Philip Mackowiak disagrees: on inspecting one of Wunderlich's original glass thermometers he found it calibrated roughly 2C high, and the cumbersome foot-long mercury instruments plus armpit-only readings make historical comparisons shaky. Parsonnet counters that her Union Army veterans data — comparing people born in different years measured at the same time, and vice versa — separates instrument effects from genuine biological change, and the same decline shows up in modern datasets using comparable thermometers.

**What shapes your own baseline:** age (older people run cooler as metabolism slows), gender (women run warmer than men, for reasons not fully understood), time of day (a circadian dip around 03:00–05:00 and a peak around 16:00–18:00), and body size (temperature falls with height due to greater surface-area heat loss, and rises slightly with weight).

**Takeaway:** 37C is losing its "exalted status" — reference works including Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine and UpToDate have already adjusted. Experts caution against treating any single threshold as a sharp boundary (36.99C is not meaningfully different from 37.01C), but note that adults dropping below about 35C (96F) or spiking above 40C (104F) is a genuine warning sign. The article carries the BBC's standard disclaimer that it is general information, not a substitute for professional medical advice.
